videos.title: Meet DOTS  the always on agent that orchestrates your entire ChatGPT.
videos.ai_tech_id: OpenAI Dots — always-on orchestration agent for ChatGPT (Pro/Enterprise rollout)
summary: The Futurepedia host introduces Dots, OpenAI's new always-on agent that sits above a user's entire ChatGPT workspace rather than living inside a single chat, positioning it as a fix for the common problem of juggling many separate conversations and work sessions.

He explains that Dots has access to the user's memories, connected tools, skills, and scheduled tasks, and can spin up new chats, work sessions, or Codex sessions on its own, including tasks that run on the user's computer while it stays powered on.

The video highlights that Dots gets its own persistent cloud computer and keeps the same conversation synced across phone and desktop, noting the feature is rolling out first to Pro and Enterprise subscribers.

videos.title: Can Humanizer make AI writing sound human?
videos.ai_tech_id: Humanizer skill (used with Claude) — AI-writing-pattern removal tool
summary: The video asks whether a tool called Humanizer can strip the telltale patterns of AI-generated writing, calling out specific cliches like the 'it's not this, it's that' construction, a stock 'welcome to system one models' closing line, and a vague 'essay vs. decision' setup that the host says show up by default in Claude's own tweets.

The host demonstrates installing the Humanizer skill and running a draft through it, showing how it rewrites the formulaic 'slop' lines into phrasing that reads more like something a person actually wrote.

The video frames the tool as most valuable on longer pieces of writing rather than short posts like tweets, suggesting it's better suited to documents, articles, or other extended text where AI-writing tics are more noticeable and more damaging to credibility.

videos.title: I Tested OpenAI's Dots vs. Meta's Muse. What You Need to Know.
videos.ai_tech_id: OpenAI Dots vs. Meta Muse — competing personal AI agent platforms
summary: Nate Herk runs a head-to-head comparison of OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, two competing always-on personal AI agents, evaluating them across features, pricing, memory handling, and third-party integrations based on hands-on use of both.

He walks through how each agent fits into existing workflows and ecosystems, including Codex, Slack, and WhatsApp, and candidly reports the bugs and limitations he ran into with each platform during testing rather than giving a purely promotional take.

The video closes with his personal verdict on which tool he'd choose, including who he thinks Muse is actually a good fit for, and his broader prediction on where personal AI agents are headed as both OpenAI and Meta push further into this space.

videos.title: 5 ChatGPT Study Codes for Notes, Quizzes, and Test Prep
summary: Sabrina Ramonov shares five short ChatGPT commands meant to turn one study topic into five different formats for exam prep, starting with /stickynotes for quick main-point notes and /questionpredictor to surface the roughly 20% of material most likely to appear on a test.

She covers two more visually- and interactively-oriented codes: /studyguide to generate a visual diagram with a step-by-step walkthrough of a topic, and /quizme, which asks one adaptive question at a time and adjusts difficulty based on the user's answers.

The fifth code, /storymode, turns the lesson into a narrative sequence, and she frames the whole set as a way to study the same topic from five angles by simply pasting a different code into ChatGPT each time.

videos.title: 3 Claude Prompts for a 20-Day Business Plan
summary: Sabrina Ramonov presents a three-prompt Claude sequence designed to move someone from a vague idea to a concrete first-income plan, starting with a prompt asking for two ways to make $1,000 in 30 days using skills the user already has, with no existing audience required.

The second prompt has Claude identify a single person the user should model their approach after, and the third asks Claude to role-play as that person and build a 20-day, sub-$1,000 plan focused on landing a first paying customer as quickly as possible, including starting outreach on day one.

She stresses keeping all three prompts in the same chat so Claude retains context, answering its follow-up questions about the user's skills, time, and budget, and then committing to testing just one resulting idea rather than overanalyzing options.

videos.title: Microsoft’s plan to win the AI race, explained
videos.ai_tech_id: Microsoft Copilot (multi-model Auto mode) with Work IQ — enterprise AI strategy
summary: Jeff Su breaks down Microsoft's strategy for the new Copilot, framing it around two pillars: letting users choose which underlying AI model handles a task (or letting an Auto mode pick one automatically) and giving Copilot deep context about the company itself.

He explains Work IQ, the piece that lets Copilot find relevant information scattered across dozens of Word documents, Teams channels, and emails, while strictly respecting each user's existing permissions so it only surfaces what they're already allowed to see.

The video frames Microsoft's overall bet as building AI for entire companies rather than individual users, pairing flexible model selection with deep organizational context, and closes by asking viewers who use Copilot at work to share their real-world experiences with the new app.
